scene.testo: Step outside the International Space Station and the temperature can swing from minus 250 degrees Fahrenheit to plus 250 degrees Fahrenheit. A five hundred degree swing. And your spacesuit has no heater switch you can flip.

Space is not simply cold. It is something stranger. The station circles Earth at 17,500 miles per hour, and every ninety minutes it rushes through a full sunrise and a full sunset, over and over again.

Imagine you are floating inside the station at 6 AM. Your sleeping bag is strapped to the wall. The air feels comfortable, around 70 degrees Fahrenheit. Outside this thin metal wall, though, the situation is completely different.
Here is the surprise that confuses almost everybody. Space itself has no temperature you can feel. It is a near vacuum, with almost nothing in it to carry heat to your skin or pull it away.

On Earth, cold is air. Wind steals your warmth by touching your skin and carrying heat away. Without air, that kind of heat loss simply stops. Heat can only leave by one slow route, and that route is radiation.
Think of a thermos bottle. It keeps coffee hot because a vacuum sits between its walls. A vacuum is a terrible conductor of heat. That is why a hot astronaut in space struggles to cool down at all.
So the first big surprise is this. Astronauts usually worry about getting too hot, not too cold. Their bodies, their computers, and their machines all produce heat, and that heat has to go somewhere.

The station is about the size of a football field, including its huge solar arrays. Its pressurized living space is closer to a big house. Every watt of electricity used inside eventually turns into heat that must be removed.

The station's trick is a pair of systems working together. Inside, water loops carry heat away from equipment and people. Outside, huge radiator panels release that heat into space as infrared light. It is a cooling system, not a heater.

Picture the radiators as the station's skin. Ammonia flows through outside pipes, carrying heat from the water loops. The ammonia then flows through the radiator panels, where the heat glows away as invisible infrared light into the dark.

Now remember the swing. When the station faces the sun, its surfaces can climb toward plus 250 degrees Fahrenheit. In the shadow of Earth, they can fall toward minus 250 degrees. So the walls need serious protection.

That protection is multi-layer insulation. Those shiny gold and silver blankets on spacecraft are not decoration. They are stacks of thin reflective layers that bounce heat away from the sun side and hold it in on the shadow side.

Many of those layers are only thinner than a human hair. Each one reflects radiant heat, and the gaps between them are vacuum. Stack enough of them and almost no heat crosses, in either direction. It is a thermos wrapped around a spacecraft.

Now step into the airlock. You are about to leave the station on a spacewalk. Your suit weighs about 300 pounds on the ground, roughly the weight of a large refrigerator. In orbit, it weighs nothing, but it is still stiff and bulky.

Your suit is a personal spacecraft. It has oxygen to breathe, pressure to keep your blood from boiling, a radio, and a cooling system. Look closely and you will find something missing. There is no heater built into the NASA suit's main design.

Under the outer layers, you wear a garment laced with plastic tubing, a bit like long underwear with spaghetti sewn into it. Cool water flows through those tubes, drawing heat from your skin. Yes, your suit is mostly about staying cool.

Heat is a real danger out there. Working hard in a pressurized suit, an astronaut can make a lot of body heat. Without that water cooling, sweat would pool inside the suit and the astronaut could overheat dangerously fast.

Outside the suit are many layers. Inside the outer cover sit layers of insulation, then a pressure bladder, then a restraint layer, and finally the liquid cooling garment against your skin. Each layer has a job, and none of them is a heater.

Still, cold is real out there, especially for your hands and feet. Space gloves have small heaters on the fingertips. Astronauts have reported cold fingers during spacewalks in the shadow, so some warmth is built in there.

The fingertip heaters exist because hands touch metal handrails that can be extremely cold after hours in shadow. Touch cold metal in a vacuum and heat drains by conduction, the one path that still works fast. Fingers suffer first.

Here is a detail that surprises people. A spacewalker can have one side of the suit baking in sunlight while the other side faces deep shadow. The suit has to cope with both at the same moment, just inches apart.

Your helmet visor is coated with a thin layer of gold. It reflects the sun's harsh glare and infrared heat while still letting you see. Gold works because it reflects heat so well, which is why it shows up on many spacecraft.

Now come back inside. A typical spacewalk lasts about six and a half hours. That is a full workday in a suit, with no break, no sandwich, and a small drink bag inside the helmet. Then you float back through the airlock.

Inside the station, the temperature is kept comfortable on purpose. Crews often describe the cabin as mild. The challenge is rarely freezing. It is that air does not rise, so warm air around your body just sits there.

On Earth, hot air rises and carries heat away through convection. In microgravity, that stops. Without fans, warm air around a person can form a bubble, and carbon dioxide can pool near your face. That is why the station has constant airflow.

Those fans are noisy. Astronauts have talked about the constant hum on the station. Sleep is hard, so many crew members use earplugs. The noise is the price of fresh air and steady temperature in a place without natural airflow.
Sleeping crews zip into bags attached to a wall or ceiling, since there is no up or down. Arms float gently in front of them. Staying warm at night is rarely the issue. Staying anchored is.

Now think about food. Meals come in pouches and cans, and many are heated in a small food warmer on the station. Hot meals matter, and crews have spoken about how much a warm dinner lifts the mood after a long day.

The warmer heats food pouches to a safe temperature, and crews can rehydrate soups and stews with hot water. Coffee is a favorite. Astronauts have used special cups designed so the drink holds its shape and flows to the lips.

Compare that to a camping trip on Earth. You huddle around a fire, boil water on a stove, and wear a puffy jacket. In orbit, the crew relies on electric systems, warm cabin air, and sealed walls instead.

Now think about the Apollo missions. In 1969 and 1972, crews flew to the Moon and back. Their spacecraft slowly rolled like a chicken on a spit, so the sun's heat spread evenly across the hull. NASA called it passive thermal control.

That barbecue roll was a clever fix. Without it, one side of the spacecraft would overheat while the other froze. A slow rotation of about once every twenty minutes evened things out, with no heater needed for the hull.

Apollo 13 is the famous case of real cold. In April 1970, after an oxygen tank failed, the crew powered down their ship to save energy. The cabin grew cold and damp, and water droplets condensed on the walls.

The crew later said they were very cold, and cabin temperatures fell to around the low 40s degrees Fahrenheit, according to NASA's accounts. They wore extra clothing and tried to rest. It was a rare moment when heat was truly missing.

Nobody planned that. Power meant heat, and the crew needed every bit of electricity to get home. That story shows how much comfort in space depends on a steady flow of energy, and what happens when it stops.

On the Moon, the numbers get extreme. Lunar daytime surface temperatures reach about 250 degrees Fahrenheit. At night, they plunge to around minus 208 degrees Fahrenheit or colder, according to NASA. Apollo astronauts worked only in daylight.

Those Moon walkers wore suits with water cooling too. Their dust-covered boots stood on ground that was baking in sunlight. Mission planners picked landing times so the sun was low, which kept the surface temperature more bearable.

Back in orbit, the station also has heaters, to be fair. Some equipment, like pumps and fluid lines, has electric heaters so it does not freeze in shadow. The point is that heating is targeted, not blasted everywhere.

Every spacecraft carries a thermal design built around one question. Where does the heat come from, and where can it go? Engineers draw maps of heat flow before launch. They call it thermal analysis, and it shapes the whole vehicle.

Before flight, spacecraft are tested in giant thermal vacuum chambers. They are pumped down to near vacuum and heated and cooled to the extremes they will face. If something cracks or fails, engineers find out on the ground.

Now flip the question around. What if an astronaut did float into space with no suit? NASA has described that it would not freeze instantly. The real danger is the lack of air and pressure, which affects the body within seconds.

So the cold of space is mostly a story about heat that cannot escape, not cold that rushes in. That is the opposite of what movies show. Your biggest enemy out there is usually trapped warmth, not frostbite.

Think back to the minus 250 degrees Fahrenheit number from the start. It describes shaded surfaces in direct view of deep space. It is real, but your suit, your station, and your ship are all designed to shrug it off.

Here is the most surprising detail of all. The thing that keeps astronauts alive in the cold of space is mostly water, flowing through tubes against their skin. So the next time you imagine space is freezing, remember that astronauts are fighting to stay cool.

descrizione:
Space is said to be freezing, with temperatures swinging from -250°F to +250°F. So how do astronauts survive without heaters? In this Orbital Days documentary, we float inside the International Space Station at 6 AM and follow a spacewalk to learn how real NASA suits, insulation, and cooling systems work.

Discover why heat in a vacuum behaves so strangely, why astronauts often fight overheating instead of cold, what the Apollo 13 crew endured, and how engineers use radiators, gold visors, and thermal blankets to protect crews orbiting at 17,500 mph.
